title: 10 Everyday English Idioms
summary: Learn 10 common English idioms that native speakers use every day. Discover what they really mean so you can sound more natural.

sections.p: English speakers often use colors to talk about how they feel. When you are sad, you might feel blue. When you receive a surprise gift or good news out of nowhere, it happens completely by surprise. These colorful phrases make daily conversations much more interesting and fun to listen to.

ex.en: I was feeling a bit blue yesterday, so I watched my favorite comedy movie.
ex.mean: I was feeling a bit sad yesterday, so I watched my favorite comedy movie.

ex.en: The job offer came out of the blue, and I was so happy.
ex.mean: The job offer happened unexpectedly, and I was so happy.

ex.en: She passed her driving test with flying colors.
ex.mean: She passed her driving test with a very high score and great success.

sections.p: Food and animals are very popular in English idioms. If you are very nervous before a big presentation, you might feel little creatures moving inside your stomach. Or, if you accidentally tell a secret that was supposed to stay hidden, you cause a big problem for everyone.

ex.en: I had butterflies in my stomach before going on stage.
ex.mean: I felt very nervous before going on stage.

ex.en: Who spilled the beans about the surprise party?
ex.mean: Who told the secret about the surprise party?

ex.en: Let's call it a day and go home.
ex.mean: Let's stop working for today and go home.

sections.p: To talk about starting a task or facing a difficult situation, native speakers use action-based expressions. Instead of speaking for a long time, someone might ask you to get straight to the main point. When you do something perfectly, you hit the target directly.

ex.en: Stop beating around the bush and tell me what you think.
ex.mean: Stop avoiding the main topic and tell me what you think.

ex.en: You hit the nail on the head with that guess.
ex.mean: You described the situation or answer completely correctly.

ex.en: Under the weather, I decided to stay in bed.
ex.mean: Feeling slightly sick, I decided to stay in bed.

ex.en: Cost an arm and a leg, but the laptop is great.
ex.mean: Was very expensive, but the laptop is great.

words.en: hit the nail on the head
cost an arm and a leg

tip: Do not translate idioms word-for-word into your native language, because they will not make sense. Instead, try to learn the whole phrase as one single idea.

quiz.ask: Choose the correct idiom for feeling sad.
quiz.en: Lately, John has been feeling ___ because his best friend moved away.

quiz.ask: Choose the correct idiom for stopping work.
quiz.en: We have worked for eight hours. Let's ___ and go home.

quiz.ask: Choose the correct idiom for revealing a secret.
quiz.en: Mark accidentally ___ about the holiday destination.

quiz.ask: Choose the correct idiom for something very expensive.
choices: cost an arm and a leg

quiz.ask: Choose the correct idiom for being nervous.
quiz.en: I always get ___ before a job interview.

quiz.ask: Choose the correct idiom for being right.
quiz.en: Your explanation of the problem really ___.
choices: hit the nail on the head
